title: Linguistic Human Rights

pts: Linguistic human rights frameworks argue individuals have a right to education in their own language, and freedom from discrimination based on language.
This extends general human-rights principles specifically into the linguistic domain, connecting directly to Unit 59's critical language awareness.
This remains a genuinely developing area of international law and advocacy, not a single, universally settled legal framework.
points.who: Tove Skutnabb-Kangas's linguistic human rights framework

v: Short extracts from Article 350A, RTE Act Section 29, NEP 2020 para 4.11 and the UN Minorities Declaration

items: Give each group one extract from a legal or policy text.
Groups rewrite it in two plain-English sentences, then in their home language.
Groups decide: who holds this right, who must act, and what would count as it being met?
Collect answers on a class chart with three columns: ‘right’, ‘duty-bearer’, ‘evidence of practice’.
Discuss where these rights are well met and poorly met in local schools.
In a DIET session, compare the national provisions with the state’s own language-in-education orders.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

body: Purpose: to break a rights provision into its working parts. Content: a three-part chain: a child holding a book (‘right-holder’), a school building with a state emblem (‘duty-bearer’) and a clipboard with a tick (‘evidence of practice’). pts: Linguicism describes discrimination based on language, paralleling other recognised forms like racism or sexism.
This connects directly to Unit 96's native-speakerism content as one specific, documented form of linguicism.
Naming this phenomenon explicitly supports more rigorous, structured critique than treating language-based discrimination as merely incidental.

items: Present eight short scenarios from school life (see model language).
Groups rate each from 0 (neutral) to 3 (clear linguicism) and justify their rating.
For each scenario rated 2 or 3, groups propose an alternative practice.
Compare the scenarios with the native-speakerism examples in Unit 96.
Participants add an anonymized scenario from their own schooling.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: A school collects a one-rupee fine each time a child speaks Kannada in the corridor.
A teacher marks ‘kindly revert’ as an error in a letter written by a Class 10 learner.
A child from a Lambani-speaking family is placed in a lower section because she is quiet in English.
The school assembly includes a thought for the day in a different language each week.
T: Why is the third one serious?
S1: Because the school judges her ability by one language.
S2: She might be clever in her own language, but nobody checks.

blocks.x: The last scenario is the opposite of linguicism: it gives every language a visible place (Skutnabb-Kangas 2000).

body: Purpose: to show practices ranging from inclusive to linguicist. Content: a horizontal scale from green to red with small icons placed along it: a multilingual noticeboard at the green end, a fine box at the red end, and a corrected exercise book in the middle. Style: simple, unemotional. Board version: a line from 0 to 3 with short labels.

pts: Debates over minority-language speakers' right to education in their own language directly connect to Unit 88's bilingualism content.
Subtractive bilingual education models (Unit 88) are sometimes explicitly critiqued through this rights-based lens.
This framework offers one influential, though contested, lens for evaluating language-in-education policy choices.

items: Present two cases: a child moved to English-medium at age six with no home-language support, and a child taught in the home language with English added gradually.
Groups predict each child’s likely outcomes at age fourteen in English, in the home language and in content learning, drawing on Unit 88.
Revisit the distinction between additive and subtractive bilingualism from Unit 88.
Discuss which route the linguistic human rights framework would support, and why.
Compare with a local mother-tongue-based multilingual education programme, such as those developed for tribal languages in Odisha [VERIFY current programme details].
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Case summaries (fictional, written for this book):

lines: Case A: Ravi, Telugu-speaking, enters an English-medium school; Telugu is not used or taught. By Class 4 he copies answers but cannot explain them.
Case B: Sunita, Santali-speaking, learns to read in Santali, then in Odia and English; her teachers use Santali to explain new concepts.

blocks.x: The rights framework treats Case A as a denial of a basic educational right; the research on bilingualism in Unit 88 suggests that Case B is also likely to produce stronger long-term academic outcomes (Cummins 2000).

body: Purpose: to contrast additive and subtractive bilingualism. Content: two plants; in the first, a new branch labelled ‘English’ grows from a strong trunk labelled with the home language; in the second, the home-language trunk is cut and an English branch is propped up on a stick. Style: gentle illustration. Board version: two simple tree shapes.

items: StoryWeaver (free, Pratham Books) for bilingual stories that support additive practice.

pts: Some scholars question whether rights language is the most effective or accurate framework for these genuinely complex, context-dependent policy questions.
Practical implementation of linguistic rights claims raises real questions about resourcing, feasibility, and competing rights in multilingual societies.
Presenting this as a genuine, unresolved scholarly and policy debate, as with Unit 59's linguistic-imperialism discussion, is the most honest approach.

v: Two short position texts; debate roles

items: Give half the class a text summarizing the rights case and half a text summarizing the critique.
Each side prepares three arguments and one likely objection.
Hold a structured debate (Unit 39) with timed turns.
Out of role, learners write what each side got right, and which disagreements are about values rather than evidence.
Run it as a ‘fishbowl’, with speakers rotating into the centre.
Support: provide argument cards and sentence frames.
Challenge: participants find a real policy case and test both positions against it.

lines: For: Education in a language a child does not understand denies her equal access to learning. This is a matter of justice, and rights language makes states accountable.
Against: Rights language assumes neat, separate languages. In real multilingual cities, children’s repertoires mix, and fixing one ‘mother tongue’ per child can be artificial and unaffordable.
Both sides want children to understand their lessons. They disagree about whether ‘rights’ is the best tool for getting there.

blocks.x: Presenting this as an open debate follows the approach of Unit 59 to linguistic imperialism (May 2012; Wee 2011).

body: Purpose: to present the rights framework and its critique as a balanced debate. Content: two speakers at a table facing each other, each with a speech bubble containing a key word (‘justice’ and ‘complexity’); between them, a child holding a book. Style: even-handed, neither speaker dominant. Board version: two columns headed ‘For’ and ‘Against’.

items: Kialo Edu (free) for mapping arguments and counter-arguments [VERIFY current availability].

blocks.x: A two-column argument map on the board.

pts: English teaching can be framed as either supporting linguistic rights (providing genuine access and opportunity) or undermining them (contributing to language shift, per Unit 94).
Both framings capture genuine, real aspects of English's complex global role — neither alone fully captures the whole picture.
This connects directly to Unit 59's linguistic-imperialism debate as a closely related, overlapping discussion.

v: Two short case studies; a T-chart

items: Present a case in which English opens access (for example, a first-generation graduate who gets a job through English).
Present a case in which English contributes to language shift (for example, a family that stops speaking Kodava at home), linking to Unit 94.
Groups complete a T-chart: ways English teaching supports rights; ways it may undermine them.
Groups propose classroom practices that keep the first column and reduce the second.
Learners interview a grandparent or neighbour about which languages the family used in the past and uses now.
Support: provide completed examples for each column.
Challenge: learners write a short opinion essay with a clear thesis.

blocks.x: A completed T-chart (written for this book):

lines: Supports rights: access to higher education, national and international jobs, information and legal documents.
Undermines rights: prestige hierarchy that devalues home languages; families abandoning the home language; exams that reward English only.
Practice that keeps the first and reduces the second: teach English well, and use and praise home languages in the same classroom.

blocks.x: Both framings describe something real; neither alone captures English’s complex role, as the linguistic imperialism debate in Unit 59 showed.

body: Purpose: to show English as both a door and a pressure. Content: a doorway labelled ‘English’ opening onto a path of opportunity; beside it, a smaller home-language house with its windows dimming. Style: symbolic, not dramatic. Board version: a door and a house side by side.

pts: Testing learners' academic content knowledge in a language they haven't yet mastered raises genuine linguistic-rights and validity concerns simultaneously.
This connects directly to Unit 21's test-validity framework — a test conflating content knowledge with language proficiency has a genuine validity problem.
This is a concrete, practical intersection between assessment theory and rights-based policy concerns.

v: Three science or social science test items in English

items: Choose three items from a recent content-subject test.
For each, identify the content knowledge tested and the English needed to access the question.
Rewrite each item to reduce unnecessary linguistic load without lowering the content demand.
Discuss other accommodations: glossaries, bilingual papers, oral responses, extra time. Link to Unit 21: a score that mixes content and language has a validity problem.
Try the original and simplified items with two parallel groups and compare results.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: An original item (written for this book):

lines: Elucidate the circumstances under which the phenomenon of evaporation is accelerated.
When does water evaporate faster? Give two conditions.
A: The first version tests ‘elucidate’ and ‘phenomenon’ as much as science.
B: And a child who knows the answer in Kannada may still get zero.

blocks.x: Shohamy (2001) and Abedi (2004) both show how tests given in a dominant language can misrepresent what minority-language learners know, a validity problem and a fairness problem at once.

body: Purpose: to show how language load can hide content knowledge. Content: a test paper under a magnifying glass; inside the lens, two overlapping bars labelled ‘science knowledge’ and ‘English needed’, making it hard to see which produced the score. Style: clear diagram. Board version: one bar split into two colours with a question mark.

body: When simplifying a test item, keep the subject-specific terms learners have been taught (such as evaporation) and remove only the general academic vocabulary and complex grammar that the item does not intend to test.

pts: Awareness of this framework supports more thoughtful advocacy for learners' genuine linguistic needs within institutional and policy constraints.
This connects directly to Unit 72's teacher-identity content — rights awareness is one input into that exercised agency.
This doesn't require becoming a rights-law expert, only a working awareness of the framework and its genuine stakes.

v: A current school practice to review

items: Choose one school practice that affects learners’ language rights (seating by medium, language fines, assembly language, test language).
Gather simple evidence: who is affected, how, and what the policy texts say.
Draft a short, respectful note to the head teacher proposing one change.
Peer-review the note for tone, evidence and feasibility.
Discuss the role of teacher agency and identity from Unit 72: what is within your influence?
In a DIET, trainees draft a note to a cluster resource coordinator about a practice seen during school visits.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Dear Madam, I would like to propose that we stop collecting fines for speaking Kannada or other home languages in school. NEP 2020 encourages the use of home languages in learning, and I have found that learners participate more when they can check ideas in their own language first. I would be glad to share a short plan for using home languages to support English lessons.

blocks.x: Rights awareness does not require legal expertise; it requires knowing the framework well enough to act thoughtfully within real constraints.

body: Purpose: to show individual teacher action as a lever for change. Content: a teacher pressing down a small lever that lifts a larger block labelled ‘school practice’; the fulcrum is labelled ‘evidence and policy’. Style: simple, confident. Board version: a seesaw with labels.

dek: Unit 97 of 100: the emerging framework treating access to education in one's own language, and freedom from linguistic discrimination, as genuine human rights.

aims.x: This unit introduces the idea that language is a matter of rights as well as of skills. The linguistic human rights framework argues that people have a right to learn through a language they understand and to be free from discrimination on the basis of language. The unit presents the framework, its critics, and what it can mean in an ordinary classroom.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: summarize the main claims of the linguistic human rights framework;
define linguicism and recognize examples of it in school life;
relate minority-language education rights to additive and subtractive bilingualism;
evaluate the main criticisms of a rights-based approach to language policy;
explain why English teaching can both support and undermine linguistic rights;
identify validity and fairness problems when content is assessed through a language learners have not mastered;
locate linguistic rights provisions in the Indian Constitution and in NEP 2020;
connect rights awareness to concrete classroom practices.

why: Why this matters. Language policy questions raised throughout this tier connect to a formal rights framework worth understanding directly, not just as abstract background.

background.x: The phrase linguistic human rights is associated above all with Tove Skutnabb-Kangas and Robert Phillipson, whose edited volume (Skutnabb-Kangas and Phillipson 1994) brought together legal, sociolinguistic and educational perspectives. The core claim is that some language rights are so basic to human dignity that they should be protected as human rights: the right to identify with one’s mother tongue, to learn it, to use it in official situations, and, crucially for education, to be taught through it, at least in the early years (Skutnabb-Kangas 2000). International instruments give partial support. The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Persons Belonging to National or Ethnic, Religious and Linguistic Minorities (1992) encourages states to provide opportunities for minorities to learn their mother tongue or to be taught in it, though in cautious, non-binding language.

Skutnabb-Kangas also coined, in the late 1980s, the term linguicism for ideologies and practices that legitimize an unequal division of power and resources between groups defined on the basis of language. The term deliberately parallels racism and sexism. It names practices often treated as natural, such as fining children for speaking their home language at school. The native-speakerism of Unit 96 is one specific form.

The framework has critics. Stephen May (2012) broadly supports minority language rights but insists on attention to context and to the difference between tolerance-oriented and promotion-oriented rights. Lionel Wee (2011) questions whether rights discourse is the best tool at all, since it tends to treat languages as fixed, countable objects and groups as clearly bounded, when real multilingual practice is fluid (see Unit 71 on translanguaging). Practical objections concern cost, the number of languages in a state, and competing claims: in a Bengaluru classroom with learners from eight home languages, whose mother tongue becomes the medium?

India offers a long-standing constitutional answer. Article 29 protects the right of any section of citizens to conserve a distinct language, script or culture; Article 30 gives linguistic minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions; and Article 350A directs states to provide facilities for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage for children of linguistic minority groups. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 asks that the medium of instruction, as far as practicable, be the child’s mother tongue, and NEP 2020 recommends the home language, mother tongue or local language as the medium of instruction until at least Grade 5, preferably till Grade 8 (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020: para 4.11). Ajit Mohanty’s (2019) work on the ‘multilingualism of the unequals’ shows how far practice still lies from these provisions, especially for tribal languages. Every English teacher works inside this gap.

items: Policy summary. A one-page plain-language summary of the linguistic rights provisions relevant to your school.
Linguicism analysis. An analysis of three practices in your context, with proposed alternatives.
Test revision. Two content test items rewritten to reduce linguistic load, with a validity rationale.
Advocacy note. A short, evidence-based proposal for one change in school practice.
Which languages do your learners bring to class, and which are visible in the school?
Have you ever penalized a learner for using a home language? What would you do now?
Do you find the rights framework or its critics more persuasive? Why?
How much of your content assessment is also, unintentionally, an English test?
What is within your power to change, and what needs collective action?

terms.def: The learning of a second language while the first language continues to be valued and developed, so that the learner gains a language rather than replacing one; for example, adding English to Kannada rather than substituting it.
Language difficulty in a test that is not part of what is being measured, such as complex English in a mathematics test, which can unfairly lower learners’ scores.

In a rights-based framework, the person or institution responsible for making a right real, such as the state or a school under the Right to Education Act, as distinct from the right-holder, the child.
The process by which a community gradually replaces one language with another in more and more domains, often over generations.
Ideologies and practices that legitimize and reproduce unequal power and resources between groups defined by language (Skutnabb-Kangas 1988); a form of linguistic discrimination.

The rights of individuals and communities to use, learn and be educated in their own languages, including the right to learn an official language; the idea is closely associated with Tove Skutnabb-Kangas and Robert Phillipson.

A group whose language differs from the dominant or official language of the region or state; India’s Constitution provides for instruction in the mother tongue for linguistic minority children at the primary stage.
Education in which the language of instruction is the learner’s first language or home language; India’s National Education Policy 2020 recommends it, wherever possible, until at least Grade 5.

A situation in which learning a second language leads to loss or weakening of the first, often when the first language has low status (Lambert 1974). It contrasts with additive bilingualism, where the first language is maintained.
A change in how a test is given, such as extra time, large print, a reader or a separate room, that removes a barrier for a learner with a particular need without changing what the test measures.
